answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**The Letter Violates 15 U.S.C. § 1692e Because the Least Sophisticated Debtor Could Reasonably Read It to Have Two or More Meanings, One of Which Is Inaccurate.**

**A. The Letter is judged through the eyes of the least sophisticated debtor.**

The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act ("FDCPA") prohibits "any false, deceptive, or misleading representation or means in connection with the collection of any debt." 15 U.S.C. § 1692e. That prohibition expressly reaches "[t]he use of any false representation or deceptive means to collect or attempt to collect any debt." *Id.* § 1692e(10). Because the statute is remedial, this Court construes its language broadly to give effect to its purpose. *Brown v. Card Serv. Ctr.*, 464 F.3d 450, 453 (3d Cir. 2006).

Communications from debt collectors are analyzed from the perspective of the least sophisticated debtor. *Id.* at 453–54. That standard is lower than the reasonable-debtor standard. A letter that would not mislead a reasonable debtor may still violate the Act. *Id.* at 454. The inquiry protects the gullible as well as the shrewd. *See id.* at 453–54; *Lesher v. Law Offs. of Mitchell N. Kay, PC*, 650 F.3d 993, 997 (3d Cir. 2011). The question therefore is not whether Plaintiff was actually deceived, or whether a careful lawyer could arrive at the correct reading. It is whether the least sophisticated debtor could be misled.

**B. A reasonable but inaccurate second reading establishes deception.**

A collection letter "is deceptive when it can be reasonably read to have two or more different meanings, one of which is inaccurate." *Wilson v. Quadramed Corp.*, 225 F.3d 350, 354 (3d Cir. 2000) (internal quotation marks omitted); *accord Brown*, 464 F.3d at 455. Plaintiff therefore need not show that the inaccurate meaning is the only meaning, or even the most natural one. The existence of an accurate reading does not cure a reasonable inaccurate one. A collector that chooses language open to both bears the consequences of that choice.

This Court has applied these principles to reject collectors' efforts to defeat liability. In *Brown*, the Court reversed dismissal where a letter warned that nonpayment "could" result in referral to an attorney and the least sophisticated debtor could be misled about whether such action was realistically contemplated. *See* 464 F.3d at 455. In *Rosenau v. Unifund Corp.*, 539 F.3d 218, 223–24 (3d Cir. 2008), a letter from a collector's "Legal Department" could be read to come from an attorney, precluding judgment on the pleadings for the collector. And in *Lesher*, letters on law-firm letterhead could mislead the debtor into believing that an attorney was involved in collecting the debt, notwithstanding a disclaimer on the reverse side. 650 F.3d at 1001–03. Literal accuracy and fine-print qualifications thus do not necessarily save a misleading communication.

**C. Plaintiff's reading is reasonable, inaccurate, and material.**

The standard does not impose liability for "bizarre or idiosyncratic interpretations," and it presumes a basic level of understanding and a willingness to read with care. *Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55 (internal quotation marks omitted). A debtor is accordingly expected to read the notice in its entirety. *Campuzano-Burgos v. Midland Credit Mgmt., Inc.*, 550 F.3d 294, 299 (3d Cir. 2008). Plaintiff's interpretation satisfies that limit.

The Letter states: **[quote operative language]**. Read as a whole, it can reasonably be understood to mean **[accurate meaning]**. It can just as reasonably be understood to mean **[inaccurate meaning]**. That second reading is false because **[facts]**. It requires no strained construction or disregard of other text; it follows from **[wording, placement, and context]**. Nothing elsewhere in the Letter clearly dispels it.

The inaccuracy is also material. *See Jensen v. Pressler & Pressler*, 791 F.3d 413, 420–21 (3d Cir. 2015) (applying a materiality requirement to § 1692e). A misstatement is material if it is capable of influencing the least sophisticated debtor's decision. *See id.* at 421. Here, the false reading could affect whether, when, or how a debtor pays or disputes the debt because **[explanation]**. *See Caprio v. Healthcare Revenue Recovery Grp., LLC*, 709 F.3d 142, 148–49 (3d Cir. 2013) (applying the least-sophisticated-debtor standard to collection notices), *abrogation of underlying premise recognized in light of Riccio v. Sentry Credit, Inc.*, 954 F.3d 582 (3d Cir. 2020) (en banc) (rejecting a written-dispute requirement under § 1692g(a)(3)).

Because the Letter permits a reasonable, material, and inaccurate reading, it violates §§ 1692e and 1692e(10).
